items.q: Which is a core job of the operating system?
options: Sharing the CPU and memory among programs and keeping them isolated from each other
Writing your application's business logic for you

explain.right: The OS schedules the CPU, manages memory and files, drives devices, and isolates programs so one can't trample another.
explain.wrong: It doesn't write your app, build the hardware, or pick your browsing; it manages and protects shared resources.

items.q: What's the key difference between a process and a thread?
options: They are two words for the same thing
Threads have isolated memory; processes share everything
Processes are faster versions of threads
Each process has its own isolated memory; threads within one process share that process's memory

explain.right: Processes are isolated (separate memory); threads live inside a process and share its memory, which is powerful but risks races.
explain.wrong: The isolation is reversed in the other options; processes and threads are not the same, nor is one just a faster version.

items.q: A single-core computer appears to run many apps 'at once'. This is best described as:
options: Concurrency — the OS rapidly switches between tasks so they all make progress
Impossible; one core can only ever run one app total

explain.right: One core juggles tasks by context-switching fast (concurrency); true parallelism (literally simultaneous) needs multiple cores.
explain.wrong: A single core isn't doing things simultaneously, but it can interleave many tasks; that's normal, not a defect.

options: Concurrency needs more cores than parallelism
Concurrency is dealing with many tasks by interleaving them; parallelism is actually executing multiple at the same instant (needs multiple cores)
Parallelism only works on a single core

explain.right: Concurrency is about structure (juggling many in-progress tasks); parallelism is about execution (literally simultaneous), which requires multiple cores.
explain.wrong: They aren't synonyms; it's parallelism that needs multiple cores, and concurrency can happen on a single core.

items.q: Why can sharing memory between threads cause bugs that separate processes avoid?
rubric: Threads in one process share the same memory/data
Two threads touching the same data at once can interleave badly (a race condition), corrupting it
Separate processes have isolated memory, so they don't share state to corrupt (and need explicit communication instead)

explain.right: Strong answers tie shared memory to race conditions when threads interleave on the same data, and note process isolation avoids that shared-state hazard.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'threads are just buggy' without the shared-memory/race-condition mechanism.
